neutral_facts.value: The accused, a husband, and his family members allegedly subjected the victim, his wife, to mental and physical trauma due to dowry demands. The victim's family had spent a significant amount on the marriage, including providing her stridhan (personal property) to the accused. After marriage, the accused and his family allegedly harassed the victim, pressurized her for more dowry, and subjected her to abuse and threats. The accused was an alcoholic and allegedly beat the victim regularly. The victim's family filed a domestic violence case against the accused's mother-in-law. The FIR was filed nearly two years after the divorce petition by the accused and six months after the domestic violence case. The FIR contained vague and general allegations without specific instances of criminal conduct. The police filed a chargesheet only against the accused, and the accused sought quashing of the proceedings. The High Court declined to quash the proceedings, but the Supreme Court held that the FIR was a counterblast to the divorce petition and domestic violence case, and the High Court should have exercised its inherent power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. to quash the proceedings.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the legal principle that the inherent power under Section 482 of the Cr.P.C. should be exercised sparingly, carefully and with caution, only where such exercise is justified by the tests laid down in the Section itself, and that the court has the power to prevent abuse of the process of the court or miscarriage of justice.
